tool_response.stdout:
The engine keeps to the same rule in ordinary turns: by default a thread's later requests send its recorded system prompt and tool descriptions byte for byte. Where it does change a sent prefix (a compaction, a rewind, a model switch, clearing old tool results, getting a refused request through, among others) it pays the same cost.

## Work that outlives a dispatch

A hook runs inside one dispatch with a budget of its own time (a `next` or `$` call in flight does not count; a `$.clock.sleep` does, so a `turn.step` generator that polls with it pays every sleep from its one budget), and `next.signal` aborts
when that dispatch is abandoned (the user interrupted, another hook settled
first, the budget ran out); anything started for the dispatch should stop
on it. Work meant to outlive a dispatch belongs elsewhere: start it from a
`session.start` hook, which fires once when the session is ready and is
awaited before the first prompt (so a `$.tool.register` awaited there is
listed by turn one), and keep it going with `$.clock.every` and
`$.clock.after`, whose timers run until cancelled or until the module
reloads. If the engine replaces the plugin's copy mid-session without the plugin having changed (the hooks worker was lost), the hook runs again in the fresh copy, its timers and state gone: a `$.prompt.submit`, `$.command.run` or `$.agent.spawn` the hook already made, with the same input, resolves to the first call's result and is not made twice. That covers a call made while the hook is still running, awaited or not, a timer of its own that fires in that time included; a call made after the hook returned (a later timer, a continuation), and one another hook makes in answer to a call of the start hook's, is made again. A subagent the engine interrupted because the copy that awaited it was lost is started again. `$.prompt.submit` queues a prompt that starts a turn of its own once the session is idle (never folded into a running turn; the call resolves as that turn starts, not when it ends), so
background work can wake a quiet session. `$.model.complete({ model, prompt })` runs one text completion with no history on the session's own client and always resolves a result (`ModelCompleteResult`), never a bare string and never a rejection over what the provider did: `isAnswered` with `text` and `usage` (a `ModelUsage`, the four token counts as the API spells them: the one shape `session.compact`'s result, `turn.complete`'s `usage` and the context breakdown's `apiUsage` report a call's cost in too), or `isAnswered: false` with a `reason`, `api-error` (with the HTTP `status` and the `error` kind, never the error's text), `empty-reply`, or `aborted` (its `timeoutMs` elapsed, or the dispatch that made the call was abandoned), `usage` on each arm; only a request the engine refuses to send (a blocked model, a bad `maxTokens`) rejects. `prompt` and `system` each take a string or a list of `{ text, cache? }` blocks (`ModelTextBlock`), sent in order as written: `cache: true` on a block keeps the request up to and including it in the prompt cache, so a mod that sends the same long opening on every call puts that text first and marks its last block, then reads `usage.cache_creation_input_tokens` on the call that wrote it and `usage.cache_read_input_tokens` on the calls that read it within five minutes (both zero: the text is under the model's minimum, or prompt caching is switched off, where the mark is dropped and the text still sent); on Bedrock, Vertex, Foundry or behind a gateway the cached text is found again only while `prompt` opens the same way, so there the fixed text leads `prompt` and is not marked in `system`; marks are not counted, and one more than the API takes comes back as `api-error` with status 400; a hook on `model.complete` is handed the request's `prompt` and `system` as strings, as it always was (a list's texts joined in order), with the lists beside them as `promptBlocks` and `systemBlocks` (`ModelCompleteInput`): the string is what the model is sent, and the marks hold as far as the leading blocks still open it, so a hook that appends keeps them and one that rewrites the opening sends unmarked text. `$.model.fork({ prompt })` asks one tool-less question over the session's own transcript as the main thread last sent it, same model and system prompt, so the API serves that prefix from its prompt cache (`usage.cache_read_input_tokens` says how much it served); its result is the same arms plus `nothing-to-fork` (a new session before its first turn, and again right after a /clear), its `aborted` the turn whose hook forked interrupted while the fork ran. A fork thinks as hard as the session does, which at `max` can be a minute for a one-line answer, so a quick side job says `$.model.fork({ prompt, effort: "low" })` (`ModelEffort`, the five levels `$.model.complete` takes): the level is the fork's alone, the main thread's own level, next request and cache entry being as after any fork, it may be over the session's own level as well as under it, and it is held to what the person and the organization allow (the organization's cap, the `maxEffortLevel` setting and the model's own levels lower it; a level `CLAUDE_CODE_EFFORT_LEVEL` names is a ceiling, which a fork may go under, and one that asks for more runs as if it had named none, as every fork does where that variable is `auto` or `unset`), so the result says beside its `usage` the `effort` the fork's last response ran at (absent when no response came back or the request carried no named level); a value that is none of the five rejects the call, as a missing `prompt` does. On a model that takes effort per message the level is stated after `prompt` and the cached prefix is read as for any fork; where effort is one setting of the whole request (any other model or provider, a conversation whose per-message effort the API refused, a session on a numeric level) a level other than the main thread's is still applied, but the first fork at it reads at most the system prompt and tools from the cache and writes the whole conversation again as an entry of its own (`usage.cache_creation_input_tokens`, billed and waited for, the longer the conversation the longer), which later forks at that level read while it lives; the main thread's entry stands. There are two ways round that cost: the person can have the session's model take effort per message, with `CLAUDE_CODE_MODEL_CAPABILITIES=per_turn_effort` in their shell or in the `env` of their user or managed settings (first-party API only, and until the API refuses it), or the fork can name no effort and ask for haste in `prompt` (that it has no tools, and should answer straight away without thinking it over), which moves nothing ahead of `prompt`, so the cache is read on every model. What these calls cost is billed to the session's credentials. A fork counts in the session's cost total and its cost and token metrics as a turn's requests do; a completion and a classification stay out of them, and a completion's `usage` is how a mod counts it (a classification answers only its label). Where OpenTelemetry logging is on, each request also logs an `api_request` event (`api_error` when it fails) naming the mod, third-party names redacted unless `OTEL_LOG_TOOL_DETAILS` is on, with `query_source` `plugin_model_complete` or `plugin_model_classify` (a fork's stays `hook_prompt`). Your `telemetry.log` hook is not handed the event of a completion or classification it made itself, and one made from a timer skips all of your own hooks; a fork's events reach every hook, its caller's too, so a hook that forks on them forks again. `$.ui.status`, `$.ui.toast` and
`$.ui.log` show state without starting a turn, `$.ui.copy({ text, surface })` puts text on the clipboard of the surface the caller names (a press hook passes `e.surface`; left out, the session's first): the terminal's through the machine's clipboard tool and OSC 52 (not sent in a VTE terminal once the tool has started, nor ever to VTE before 0.53), resolving `{ isCopied: true }`; `{ isCopied: false, reason }` on a remote surface, or when no tool ran and OSC 52 was not written, as in VTE before 0.53 with no clipboard tool, `no-clipboard`, or with nothing drawing, `no-surface`; the event `ui.copy` carries the target `surface`, so a hook may rewrite, refuse or take it), `$.ui.notify(text, { title })` raises a native notification by the person's own channel (their `preferredNotifChannel` setting, after their classic `Notification` hooks ran reading `plugin_notification`; headed by the plugin's name when no title is given), resolving `{ isSent: true, channel }`, or `{ isSent: false, reason }`: `disabled` when they turned notifications off, `no-channel` when their terminal has none, `no-surface` where the session holds no terminal (a `-p` run, the SDK, the desktop: the hooks alone run) or none is bound yet or the process is exiting (a call at the module's load, or in a `session.end` hook after a SIGTERM: nothing runs), `refused` when a hook on `ui.notify` answered `{ value }` without sending (a hook's `{ deny }` rejects the call instead); `terminal_bell` as the channel means a bell alone, no text shown; `$.store` keeps values
across sessions, `$.session.version()` answers the engine's `version`, its `base` release and its `builtAt` build time (the values the engine's own analytics rows carry, in every mode and build), and `$.process.run` runs a host command by argv. `$.fs` reads (text, or `{ as: 'bytes' }` for `{ base64 }`), writes, lists and stats paths; `$.fs.stat(path, { resolve: true })` also answers `realPath`, every symbolic link and `..` resolved (what `realpath` gives: a hard link, a `/.vol/` file-id spelling or a case alias keeps its own spelling), so a guard's robust form is an allow-list on `realPath` under a root it resolved the same way, and a deny-list on spellings is best effort.

`$.ui.view({ agentId })` puts an agent's transcript in the main view, as the
person's own switch from the tasks list does; `agentId` is the agent's `id`
in `$.agent.list()`, and `$.ui.view({})` goes back to the main conversation.
It moves the view only while the call answers the person's own input (a
Button they pressed, a field or a pick of theirs, a prompt or command they
typed), because the viewed agent takes the prompt's next Enter; from a
timer, a load or a turn it resolves `{ deny: 'not person-initiated' }`. It
resolves `{}` once the view shows the agent, or `{ deny }` saying why not:
no agent holds the id, the tasks list shows the person no row for it, the
agent is a teammate that was stopped or runs in a terminal pane of its own,
the view was switched again meanwhile, or the session draws no main view
(`-p`, a headless host). An argument that is neither `{}` nor `{ agentId }`
rejects. A `Pane` or `AbovePrompt` hook reads the view in force as
`e.props.view`.

`$.ui.selection()` answers what the person last selected with the mouse in
the fullscreen terminal, `{ text, requestId? }`: the text as a copy would
take it, and the transcript row it lies in, by the id that row's `ui.render`
reads as `e.requestId` (absent when it spans several rows or lies outside
the transcript). A key or a click takes the highlight down before a command
or a press runs, so the answer stays what they last selected until they
select again, dismiss it, or their next prompt or command has run: a command
they type, or a Button they press, reads it. A prompt typed while a turn
runs and folded into that turn is no run of its own: the selection stays
kept until the next one has run. In a session a host runs headless (the
desktop app) the answer is what the person has selected in the host's page,
asked of every attached client that said it answers selection reads, the
first selection to arrive taken. It
resolves `undefined` with nothing selected, and wherever the engine sees no
selection (fullscreen off, `-p`, a remote surface whose client answers no
selection reads). A command that quotes the selection into the prompt:

```js
export function register(on) {
  on('session.start', async ($, e, next) => {
    await $.command.register({
      name: 'quote',
      description: 'Quotes the selection into the prompt.',
    })
    return next(e)
  })
  on('command.run', { command: 'quote' }, async $ => {
    const selected = await $.ui.selection()
    if (selected === undefined) return { text: 'Nothing is selected.' }
    const quoted = selected.text.replace(/^/gm, '> ')
    await $.prompt.fill({ text: quoted + '\n\n', mode: 'insert' })
    return { text: 'Quoted the selection.' }
  })
}
```

`$.prompt.fill` leaves the caret past the text for `insert` and at the end for `replace` and `append`. Pass `cursor` to stand it elsewhere: an offset into the whole draft after the write, counted as the `cursor` it answers with, whatever the `mode`. An offset out of range clamps. `$.prompt.fill({ text: 'Dear ,', cursor: 5 })` leaves the person typing the name.

To repaint between keys, on a timer or a model's answer, `$.prompt.paint({
text, decorations })` sets this mod's own decorations and touches nothing
else. It answers `isPainted: false`, with the box as it stands, when the draft
no longer reads `text`, or the mod may not read it, so call `$.prompt.read`
too. With another mod hooking `prompt.read` it always answers false, painted
or not. An empty list clears. Other mods' paint stands. The draft's next change
drops it, so a timer repaints after every key.

## Tools and agent types the model can call

`$.tool.register` declares a tool: its name, the description the model
reads and its input schema; the tool is listed as `mcp__<plugin>__<name>`.
The engine places it behind ToolSearch, as it does an MCP server's tool: the
model sees its name and loads the schema when it asks. `isDeferred: false` in
the spec puts the schema in the prompt's tool list from the start, which is
what a mod whose own tool the model should reach for wants; a `tool.describe`
hook's `isDeferred` is read ahead of the spec's.
The plugin serves it by hooking `tool.call` with the matcher
`{ tool: 'mcp__<plugin>__<name>' }` and returning the result, and a call
no hook answers fails saying so. Registering the same name again replaces
the tool, and a plugin may register several, each listed as it lands. `$.agent.register` declares an agent type the same way, `<plugin>:<name>`, from an agent definition as settings JSON spells one (prompt, tools, model, and the rest, all in force); a plugin folder's `agents/*.md` files declare them too. `$.agent.spawn({ subagentType })` runs one and its answer is its `turn.complete`; an `agent.offer` hook returning `{ isOffered: false }` keeps it from the model while the plugin's own spawn still runs it.

skogix — this is a good fit for mods, and your machine already has what it needs. I checked:

- **Hooks:** the mod API can react to tool calls (`git commit`, test runs, failed Bash exit codes), new prompts and finished turns. It can draw a pane beside the chat, or a band above the prompt, that redraws whenever state changes.
- **Local LLM:** ollama is running on `:11434` with `llama3.2` (2 GB) and `gemma4` (6.6 GB) installed. A mod can call it with `$.http.fetch`, so the pets' work runs locally and costs no Claude tokens.
- **Shell jobs:** `$.process.run` lets a pet run real commands like tests or formatters, and `$.clock.every` lets it work in the background.

Your CLAUDE.md says to plan before non-trivial work, so here's the plan before I build.

## Plan: `skogpets` mod (v1)

**1. Reactions (pure hooks, no LLM)**
| event | detected via | pet mood |
|---|---|---|
| commit lands | `tool.call` Bash, `git commit` exit 0 | happy, +XP to all |
| tests green | Bash matching test runners, exit 0 | proud, +XP |
| tests red | same, exit ≠ 0 | upset, -mood for all |
| any command fails | Bash exit ≠ 0 | worried |
| long idle | `$.clock` | sleepy |

The XP, levels and moods carry over between sessions in `$.store`, so the pets grow over time.

**2. A pane beside the chat:** a small ASCII sprite per pet, its mood, an XP bar, and one speech-bubble line saying what it just did. It falls back to a single band above the prompt when the terminal is narrower than 110 columns.

**3. Each pet has a job, starting with two:**
- **Scribe** (`llama3.2`): every 5 turns, it summarizes the latest exchanges into `memory/pet-digest.md`. That file is append-only, which fits SKOGAI.md's dump-file idea.
- **Tester**: after edits, it runs the project's test command in the background and reacts. I'll leave a formatter pet for v2.

**4. Commands:** `/pets` shows stats and `/pet <name>` lets you pet one.

Files go in `/skogai/claude/dev-mods/6cbcc33f-d664-4665-b241-42c9a3c7c9c0/skogpets/`, with a `*.test.ts` run by `claude plugin test`. Once you approve, Claude Code asks once whether to turn on the mods I write in this session.

## What I'd push back on / need from you

1. **Scope of the Scribe's input.** The pet would read our transcript and pass it to a local model. It all stays on this machine, but I'd still have it read only the last few turns, not the full history.
2. **Writing into the repo.** If the Scribe writes `memory/pet-digest.md` here, it creates noise in git. Should it go to that file, or to a separate pets folder outside the repo?
3. **Tester trigger.** Which test command should it run? `package.json` exists but I didn't see a real test suite. I'd start by having pets only *react* to tests you or I run, and add the autonomous runner once there's a suite.
4. **Art style.** I can use plain ASCII critters or Unicode block sprites in the style of the `design/` pixel look. I'd start with ASCII and move to blocks later.

Say go ahead, with any corrections, and I'll build v1.
